newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai budget cuts seen hitting construction firms.
newsitem.headline: Thai budget cuts seen hitting construction firms.

text.p: Thai government plans to curb infrastructure spending in 1997 could signal tougher times ahead for local construction firms who would be chasing fewer projects, industry executives and analysts said on Friday.
To address a potential spending deficit this fiscal year, Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan proposed a 40 billion baht ($1.53 billion) reduction in infrastructure spending earlier this week.
The cuts, yet to be approved by cabinet, would see state spending on infrastructure, previously forecast at some 362 billion baht in 1997, reduced by 11 percent.
Government spending contributes some 40-60 percent of all construction revenues, according to analysts.
The future of Bangkok's planned second airport, worth some 100 billion baht or five percent of total state infrastructure spending over the next five years, is also in doubt.
The possibility of lower state spending also reduced potential corporate growth prospects, analysts said.

"Though it is hard to say exactly what will be affected, in general it looks like new projects may face cancellation and existing projects could be delayed," Philip Utsch, senior analyst at HG Asia, told Reuters.
"Projects could also be spread out over a longer period of time so company cash flow will then be affected," he said.
The cuts, although potentially damaging, will also place greater emphasis on private project financing for projects still destined to go ahead, executives said.

"Some of the big projects might get cancelled but they will probably push as much responsibility as possible onto contractors," said Rob Gregory, assistant to the president at construction company Ch Karnchang Plc.
"We are likely to see more turnkey contracts, more concessions and more privatisation in general ... the stakes are getting bigger," he said.

Thailand's largest builders such as Italian-Thai Development Plc and Ch Karnchang Plc, or those with easiest access to cheap financing, were best equipped to adapt to the changing environment, analysts said.

"Greater use of turnkey contracts for smaller projects (in the 500-800 million baht range) will (be) ... at the expense of the smaller contractors who compete for those projects now but who could not afford to finance them," said a recent report by Thaimex Finance and Securities.
Should the amount of available business fall below previous projections the largest companies will once again look at competing on smaller projects, company officials said.
Smaller contractors, including some 50 unlisted companies qualified to bid on state projects, are then likely to bear the brunt of the cuts, they said.
"We, and other big firms always have the option, albeit risky, of expanding overseas," said Gregory.

"If some of the big projects get cut we could see us and Italian-Thai bidding for projects worth 400-500 million baht which capacity has kept us away from. The further down it goes, the bigger the squeeze will be," he said.
